question: How can the practical programming component of an introductory computational linguistics course be organised without teaching several languages or building infrastructure?
hypothesis: A single Python toolkit built as courseware, with consistent simple modules, documentation and graphical demos, serves assignments, class demonstrations and projects better than a mix of languages.
contributions: NLTK: open source Python modules, tutorials and problem sets for symbolic and statistical NLP, interfaced to annotated corpora
Use in a graduate course (CIS-530, University of Pennsylvania)

method.summary: Describes a Python toolkit of independent modules (token, tree, probability, parsers, taggers, fsa, classifiers, visualization, type checking) with tutorials, auto-generated reference docs and technical reports. Evaluated informally by use in one course.

datasets.name: CIS-530 course cohort
datasets.source: University of Pennsylvania graduate class, some advanced undergraduates

inference.samples: none: one course offering, qualitative report

other.naive_bayes_and_maxent: maxent trained by Generalized Iterative Scaling or Improved Iterative Scaling; no settings given
other.type_checking: can be turned off with no performance penalty

baselines: multi-language course setups (Prolog, Perl, finite-state toolkit)
eval.protocol: qualitative instructor and student experience; course had five assignments, two exams and a final project

results.claim: The course required five assignments, two exams and a final project built on NLTK.
results.setup: CIS-530, graduate introductory computational linguistics, University of Pennsylvania, one semester
results.quote: Students were required to complete ﬁve assign- ments, two exams, and a ﬁnal project.

results.claim: Authors report a very positive experience; students valued documentation, home use and intuitive interfaces (no quantitative data).
Difficulties: finding large clean corpora, and NLTK modules finished only one or two weeks before use, forcing repeated downloads.

limits: No quantitative evaluation, no control group, single course offering; feedback is informal.
Toolkit was under active development during the course; module list is from 2002 (HMMs, language modelling, TAG listed as future work).
Not comprehensive or optimised by design (stated non-requirements).
Corpora for assignments were a stated gap.
